title: v5-haiku verdict: weaker model = MORE hardness (3.7×) but ON STILL did more work. Forced context is net-negative ACROSS models. Opt-in is the only viable design.
summary: Tested the user's hypothesis: a weaker model (haiku) has higher hardness, so recorded context should help more. Ran v5-grounded (precise+retrievable answer, --consult=search) on haiku, n=5, both arms solved 5/5 (fair). HALF CONFIRMED: H_off rose from opus 2,023 → haiku 7,444 (3.7× — weakness genuinely raises hardness). BUT FALSIFIED THE RESCUE: H_on=9,719 STILL > H_off=7,444 — the ON arm did MORE work even on the weak model, because the note-engagement overhead (retrieve → reason about applicability → apply carefully) ALSO scaled with the model's verbosity (ON output 10,027 vs OFF 7,776). METRIC −26,086, NO-WIN. ROBUST CROSS-MODEL FINDING (now confirmed on opus=strong AND haiku=weak, 5 task designs): FORCING an agent to retrieve+apply a precise note consistently makes it do MORE work than just solving directly — the consult-then-apply path costs more than the direct path, regardless of model strength or task hardness. The win-regime for forced single-task context is effectively empty. KEY DESIGN CONCLUSION: the orchestrator must make context OPT-IN, NEVER forced. Every forced-consult run (v2,v3,v4,v5,v5-haiku) showed net cost; the one opt-in run (v1) where a free agent SKIPPED consultation was neutral (no penalty). So: lean opt-in retrieval the agent invokes only when IT judges the task needs it → worst case neutral (skipped), best case the rare genuine shortcut. Forcing it guarantees the over-engagement penalty. Single-task work-reduction value is now robustly DISPROVEN; the remaining unfalsified value is compounding/coordination/parallelism (not measurable by a single-task bench). The benchmark line is conclusively done.
